paras: The attempted lynching of King Wrightman and Thompson was a mob's pursuit, in August 1903, of a Black man, King Wrightman, and a white man named Thompson, who were accused of assaulting a white widow, Mrs. Mathis, at Hartsfield in Colquitt County, Georgia. An Albany dispatch of August 14 reported both men hanged together, but Albany officials denied it that night and said the two were in jail at Moultrie. Papers noticed the case because a white man and a Black man were said to have been lynched together, and some kept printing that version after the denial.

Hartsfield was described as a "little village" about sixty miles from Albany. According to the wire reports, two men called Mrs. Mathis to her door on a Saturday night, seized her and dragged her into the yard, and she named Thompson and Wrightman as her assailants.

In the first dispatches, a posse formed as soon as the assault was reported; Wrightman hid in the swamps of Dougherty and Colquitt counties, while Thompson stayed at home. On the afternoon of August 13 a posse, seven men by the Pickens account, captured Wrightman in Dougherty County, ten miles south of Albany. That version said the men then took Thompson from his house and hanged both from one tree outside Hartsfield, and that because each accused the other, the mob hanged both "to make sure."

Later reports from Albany told a different story. On the night of August 14 officials said that officers had eluded "a mob which had been in pursuit of the negro" and placed both men safely in jail at Moultrie. An August 15 dispatch added that a mob had "tried to hang both of them, but the sheriff succeeded in taking his prisoners to Moultrie," where both were held on the assault charge. The Louisville Courier-Journal said the lynching report had come through "apparently reliable sources" but that "cooler heads" had prevented it.
The last reports left both men in the Moultrie jail under charge; no report of an indictment, trial or release was found, nor of any action against the men who pursued them.

The first dispatch ran on August 14 and 15 under headlines such as "Double Lynching" in the San Antonio Daily Light, "A Mob Swings Two" in the Raleigh News & Observer and "Hanged Both to Make Sure of the Right Man" in the Worcester Spy. The News & Observer's subhead, "One White, One Black, for the Same Abominable Crime," treated the assault as established. The denial appeared the same day elsewhere: the Savannah Morning News, the one Georgia paper in the coverage, headed it "No Men Lynched Say Albany Officers." Even in correcting the story, the Daily Kennebec Journal called the men "White and Black Assaulters of Aged Woman," and the Courier-Journal noted that the mob "Was Willing, Though, To Hang a Negro and a White Man, Too."

The Indiana Tribüne, a German-language Indianapolis paper, printed the lynching report and the denial together. On August 20 the Pickens Sentinel-Journal in South Carolina printed the fullest lynching account, with no mention of the denial, while the Bamberg Herald in the same state ran a one-line note of the denial on August 20 and again on August 27. On August 23 the Washington Times still treated the double hanging as fact, joking that the mob "drew the clothes line rather than the color line."

The only Black-press item found was a brief dispatch in the Baltimore Afro-American on August 22, its heading surviving in the scan as "From Lynchers." It carried only the officials' denial and the report that the men had been placed safely in the Moultrie jail, without comment.

The first Albany dispatch and its reprints said both men were hanged on August 13, while Albany officials, the Courier-Journal and the August 15 dispatch said both were alive in the Moultrie jail. The denial is the better-supported account: it came later, from officials, named the jail and was followed by a dispatch describing the men as held and charged, whereas the first report conceded that full details had not been received.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of King Wrightman and Thompson
bases: A mob pursued a Black man and a white man accused of assaulting a white woman and, by the later reports, tried to hang them before officers jailed them at Moultrie (A4, A5, A7); the first wire said both were hanged (A1, A20).

The first Albany wire said both men were hanged (A1, A6, A20), but Albany officials denied it the same night and later dispatches placed both alive and charged in the Moultrie jail after a mob tried to hang them (A4, A5, A7); the size of that mob is not given in the denial version (the seven-man posse appears only in the lynching version, A20).
The lynching report (A1, A6, A10, A20) is contradicted by the officials' denial and a follow-up dispatch placing both men in jail (A4, A5, A7, A25); the denial is later, official and more specific.

framing.detail: First-day headlines 'Double Lynching', 'A Mob Swings Two ... for the Same Abominable Crime', 'Hanged Both to Make Sure of the Right Man' present the assault and the mob's reasoning as fact.
Denial headlines 'No Men Lynched Say Albany Officers' and 'Jail Protects Them'; the Kennebec Journal calls the men 'Assaulters of Aged Woman'.
Courier-Journal: 'A Georgia Lynching Prevented by Cool Heads. Mob Was Willing, Though, To Hang a Negro and a White Man, Too.'
Washington Times quip after the denial that the mob 'drew the clothes line rather than the color line'.
Baltimore Afro-American runs the officials' denial as a short special dispatch, heading partly lost ('From Lynchers'), no comment.
